passages.t: A jealous and avenging God, slow to anger
passages.happening:
‘This is the burden against Nineveh, the book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite’ (verse 1). ‘The LORD is a jealous and avenging God; the LORD is avenging and full of wrath’ (verse 2). He takes vengeance on his foes. ‘The LORD is slow to anger and great in power; the LORD will by no means leave the guilty unpunished’ (verse 3). His path is in the whirlwind and storm.

He rebukes the sea and dries up the rivers. Bashan, Carmel and Lebanon wither (verse 4). Mountains quake and hills melt before him (verse 5). Who can stand before his anger (verse 6)? ‘The LORD is good, a stronghold in the day of distress; He cares for those who trust in Him’ (verse 7). But with an overwhelming flood he will make an end of Nineveh (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Nahum spoke between the fall of Thebes, about 663 BC, and the fall of Nineveh in 612 BC. For most of that time Assyria ruled the Near East, and Judah, under Manasseh and then Amon, was its vassal, paying tribute and living in its shadow.

The book's first word, burden or oracle, was a common heading for a prophet's word against a nation. The opening hymn draws on pictures shared across the ancient world, where storm gods were said to ride the clouds and rebuke the sea; Israel's poets used them to say that the LORD alone commands the forces others worshiped. Bashan, Carmel and Lebanon were the most fertile and forested regions of the land. If even they wither, nothing can stand.

Many scholars see in verses 2 to 8 a partial alphabet poem, each line beginning with the next Hebrew letter, though the pattern is irregular. The hymn is framed by God's character: jealous and avenging at the start, good and a stronghold in the middle, with the line from God's words to Moses at Sinai set within it.
passages.later: God made his name known to Moses as the one who ‘will by no means leave the guilty unpunished’ (Exodus 34:7), the same line Nahum sets beside slow to anger. A psalm also pictures the LORD's voice over the storm (Psalm 29:3).
passages.hard:
How can a good God be described as avenging and full of wrath?

Many readers are uncomfortable with a God who takes vengeance. In the Bible vengeance is a legal idea: the act of a just ruler who defends the wronged and punishes the wrongdoer, not the spite of a wounded pride. The chapter balances wrath with patience and goodness: God is slow to anger (verse 3) and a stronghold for those who trust him (verse 7). And the object of God's wrath is an empire known from its own records for mass deportation, torture and plunder. A God indifferent to that would not be good.

Some readers still find the intensity of the language troubling, and note that the Bible holds a wider picture, including God's mercy to Nineveh in Jonah. Others say that Assyria's victims would have heard Nahum's words as the long-awaited assurance that their suffering mattered to God. Both responses take the text seriously, and neither needs to pretend that God's wrath is simple to understand. Vengeance here belongs to God, and it gives no one a warrant to take it for themselves.
passages.asks: The same hymn calls God avenging and a stronghold for those who trust him. Ask which of those you find harder to believe. And ask what it means to you that God does not leave the cruelty of the powerful unanswered.

passages.t: A yoke broken, and good news on the mountains
passages.happening:
Whatever Nineveh plots against the LORD, he will bring to an end, and trouble will not rise a second time (verse 9). From Nineveh has come one who plots evil against the LORD (verse 11). Though they are strong and many, they will be cut down. Though God afflicted Judah, he will afflict it no more (verse 12). ‘For I will now break their yoke from your neck and tear away your shackles’ (verse 13).

The LORD has commanded that Nineveh will have no descendants to carry on its name, and he will cut off its carved images from the house of its gods (verse 14). ‘Look to the mountains’, comes the cry, to ‘the feet of one who brings good news, who proclaims peace’ (verse 15). Judah is to keep its feasts and its vows, for the wicked will never again march through it.
passages.hearers:
The verses turn back and forth between Nineveh and Judah, and the turns can be abrupt, because the speaker moves from one audience to the other without warning. Translations add names, O Nineveh, O Judah, to help.

The plotter of evil may recall Sennacherib, whose envoys mocked the God of Israel when he besieged Jerusalem in 701 BC, or it may describe Assyrian kingship in general. The broken yoke fits the years when Assyria began to crack. Kings in the ancient world set great store by their name and descendants, and Assyrian kings filled their palaces and temples with inscriptions and statues to keep their memory. God says Nineveh's name will not be carried on.

Verse 15 brings a scene every reader knew: a runner coming over the hill with news. In the Hebrew Bible it is 2:1, opening the next section; English Bibles end chapter 1 with it.
passages.later: Isaiah has almost the same words: ‘How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of those who bring good news, who proclaim peace’ (Isaiah 52:7). Paul quotes Isaiah's form for those sent to preach (Romans 10:15). Sennacherib's envoys mocked the LORD at Jerusalem's walls (2 Kings 18:28-35).
passages.asks: For Judah, the news of Nineveh's fall was news of peace. Ask what yoke you long to see broken, in your own life or in your world. And ask how you would carry good news to someone still living under a heavy one.
